title: Channel Coding & Error Detection/Correction
summary: Noisy channels, channel capacity, and the codes actually used in practice (parity, checksums, Hamming codes) — how data survives a lossy link.

slides.markdown:
Every real communication link — a cable, a disk, deep-space radio — is a **noisy channel**: bits sent aren't guaranteed to be the bits received. Some fraction randomly flip.

![Sender, noisy channel, and receiver, with encoding added before transmission](assets/noisy-channel-model.svg)

The fix isn't a perfect channel (impossible) — it's structured **redundancy** before transmission, so the receiver can detect or correct flips after.

assets.alt: Sender, noisy channel, and receiver, with encoding added before transmission

slides.subTitle: Channel capacity
slides.markdown:
**Shannon's noisy-channel coding theorem** says every noisy channel has a **capacity** `C` (bits/use) — a hard ceiling on reliable transmission rate. Below `C`, codes exist making the error rate arbitrarily small. Above `C`, no code can make communication reliable.

The striking part: reliability isn't a losing battle against noise, as long as you stay under `C` and add the right redundancy.

This parallels the source coding theorem directly: one sets a floor for compression, the other a ceiling for reliable transmission.

slides.subTitle: Parity bits
slides.markdown:
A **parity bit** is the simplest error-detection code: append one bit so the total number of 1s is even (or odd, by convention). The receiver recomputes parity and flags a mismatch as corruption.

Its blind spot: parity detects **any odd number** of bit flips (1, 3, 5...) but is **blind to an even number** (2, 4...) — two flips cancel out and parity still checks out, silently passing corrupted data.

This is why parity alone is only used where errors are rare and independent — anywhere burst errors are common, it's not enough on its own.

slides.subTitle: Checksums and CRC
slides.markdown:
**Checksums** sum data (mod some number) into a fixed-size value; a mismatch signals corruption. **CRC (cyclic redundancy check)** is a stronger variant using polynomial division, catching far more error patterns (all single-bit errors, most bursts) than a simple checksum.

CRC is what real link-layer protocols use (Area 4 `link-layer`) — cheap in hardware, and far better at catching real burst-error patterns than parity or naive checksums.

Neither CRC nor checksums **correct** errors — they only **detect** them, triggering a retransmission.

slides.subTitle: Hamming distance
slides.markdown:
**Hamming distance** between two equal-length bit strings is the number of positions where they differ. A code's **minimum distance** `d_min` determines what it can do:

- Detect up to `d_min - 1` bit errors.
- **Correct** up to `floor((d_min-1)/2)` errors — map a received string to the *nearest* valid codeword.

The entire theory in one idea: spread valid codewords far enough apart that a few flips can't confuse one for another.

slides.subTitle: Hamming(7,4)
slides.markdown:
**Hamming(7,4)** encodes 4 data bits using 3 parity bits (7 total), each parity covering a different, overlapping subset of data bits.

![Three overlapping parity circles, each covering a subset of data bits](assets/hamming-code-venn.svg)

On receiving, recompute all three checks: which ones fail pinpoints **exactly which bit** flipped, letting the receiver fix it — no retransmission needed.

assets.alt: Three overlapping parity circles, each covering a subset of data bits

slides.markdown:
Both spend redundancy, but on different goals.

| | Detection only (parity/CRC) | Correction (Hamming, Reed-Solomon) |
|---|---|---|
| Redundancy needed | Low | Higher |
| Recovery | Requires retransmission | Fixes in place, no retransmit |
| Best when | Retransmission is cheap (network) | Retransmission is impossible/costly (deep space, storage) |

Decide by whether you can ask the sender to resend: if yes, cheap detection + retry usually wins; if no (or retry is too slow), pay for correction upfront.

This machinery is everywhere, often invisibly: **RAID** (parity across disks reconstructs a failed drive), **network packets** (CRC in Ethernet/TCP), **QR codes** (Reed-Solomon correction, tolerating a torn corner), and **ECC memory** (Hamming-style codes fixing single-bit flips from cosmic rays, without crashing).

Each picks a point on the detection-vs-correction spectrum matched to its failure mode — a torn QR code needs correction (no "ask for a resend"); a TCP packet just needs cheap detection plus retransmission.

slides.subTitle: Redundancy isn't free
slides.markdown:
More error-correction redundancy always improves reliability — but it also **shrinks effective bandwidth**, since some of every transmitted bit is overhead. Hamming(7,4) spends 3 of every 7 bits (43%) on parity just to correct one bit.

The trade-off: over-provisioning for a clean channel wastes bandwidth/storage; under-provisioning for a noisy one causes frequent failures.

Good design matches the **code rate** (payload / total bits) to the channel's actual, measured error rate — not a worst-case guess.
